ai_technology: DorsalNet; learned neural visual model and gradient-based stimulus synthesis

evidence.ai_role: DorsalNet, trained on self-motion from naturalistic videos, enabled stimulus synthesis selectively separating early or late model-layer responses. Human tests supplied new behavioral evidence relevant to competing perceptual-learning accounts.
evidence.tested: Nineteen observers trained for three days. Late-stage-group sensitivity increased (n=10; paired p=0.001); early-stage-group change was not significant (n=9; p=0.100), while its response criterion changed. Transfer across location and stimulus type informed comparisons with alternative model readouts.
evidence.unknown: A difference in within-group significance does not itself prove a between-group learning interaction. Separate groups may differ before training; stimulus-to-cortical-stage correspondence was inferred from the model rather than directly measured. Model–human specificity agreement was assessed qualitatively, and energetic interpretations remain speculative.

organization: McGill University; Université de Montréal; Mila

source_review.scope: Primary 30-page preprint PDF: relevant stimulus-generation and observer Methods, sensitivity and transfer Results, model-comparison and causal limitations; bioRxiv API version history. Supplement not audited.

summary: A November 24, 2026 preprint used the learned DorsalNet visual model to design motion stimuli targeting different model stages, then tested training in 19 human observers. After three days, ten observers trained on late-stage stimuli showed increased perceptual sensitivity, while nine trained on early-stage stimuli mainly changed response bias. Transfer tests and model comparisons were consistent with a late-stage readout account. Cortical stages were not directly recorded, and separate participant groups limit causal comparison.
title: AI-designed visual stimuli probe how perceptual learning changes decisions
